purpose: phase-3 source scouting: sovereign yields, memory share, NAND pricing
collectionMethod: WebSearch (allowed_domains not used — broad queries against public search) for candidate discovery + citation snippets; WebFetch attempted once per host for the most promising government/statistical CSV endpoints and for TrendForce/DRAMeXchange press pages. Every WebFetch call in this sandbox returned error_type=EGRESS_BLOCKED at the network proxy layer (fred.stlouisfed.org, home.treasury.gov, www.mof.go.jp, data-api.ecb.europa.eu, www.bankofengland.co.uk, www.trendforce.com, dramexchange.com — all blocked). This is a sandbox-side block, not evidence the target server itself rejects the request (contrast with a 403/405). No candidate below was directly HTTP-verified from this session; all statuses are 'untested' unless a WebSearch snippet itself surfaced live page content (noted as 'search-indexed', a weaker positive signal — it shows a crawler could reach the page recently, not that a GitHub Actions datacenter IP can). A CI probe script with real egress must make the final call.

candidates.name: FRED fredgraph.csv (per-series CSV, US daily constant maturity)
candidates.historyDepth: Full series history from inception (DGS10 back to 1962-01-02); two columns DATE,DGS10, missing days marked '.'
candidates.headersRequired: None documented; no API key. Polite User-Agent recommended but not required — this is the plain graph-export CSV used by browsers, not the fred/api key-gated JSON API.
candidates.evidence: Multiple independent sources (ivo-welch.org FRED CSV Gateway writeup, FRED help docs, general familiarity with the FRED graph-export mechanism) describe this exact URL shape as the key-less CSV download used by scrapers; WebFetch to fred.stlouisfed.org was sandbox-blocked so the live response was not observed this session.
candidates.notes: Swap id= for DGS2 / DGS30. Update cadence: next business day after each print (Treasury constant-maturity daily series). This is the strongest single candidate for the US leg.

candidates.name: FRED fredgraph.csv — OECD MEI long-term (10y) government bond yield, per country
candidates.historyDepth: OECD MEI-sourced, typically multi-decade monthly history per country (varies by country, generally 1980s/1990s onward)
candidates.headersRequired: Same as DGS10 above — none documented.
candidates.evidence: FRED series pages confirmed via search to exist under exactly these mnemonics (IRLTLT01<CC>M156N), each labeled 'Long-Term Government Bond Yields: 10-Year: Main (Including Benchmark)', source OECD.
candidates.notes: Important finding: this single CSV pattern is the only candidate that covers all six target countries' 10y yield through one key-less mechanism. Caveat: MONTHLY frequency (OECD MEI), not daily, and 10y only — no 2y/30y for the non-US countries via this route. Treat as the cross-country baseline/fallback tier; use country-primary sources below for daily granularity and 2y/30y.

The IADB CSV route above is scraper-friendly IF the right series codes are found; the spreadsheet route is richer but likely not zero-dependency-parseable. Probe should try the IADB CSV route first and only fall back to noting the XLSX route as curated/manual.

SK hynix ... 28.8%... Micron ... 22.4%' from https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20260601-13070.html), meaning a crawler reached and indexed the full page text recently. Direct WebFetch to www.trendforce.com was sandbox-blocked this session, so live reachability from a GitHub Actions IP is not confirmed.

memory-share.reasoning: The share numbers themselves ARE published free (TrendForce press-center marketing pages, Counterpoint insight blog) and are technically fetchable key-lessly with a plain HTTP GET — this is not a hard paywall like the DRAMeXchange intelligence portal. But the data arrives as inconsistent narrative prose embedded in HTML, not a stable table/JSON schema, and publication cadence/wording varies release to release. A Node scraper could attempt best-effort regex extraction as a secondary/flagged signal, but given this repo's standing rule that 'every conclusion must be fact-verification based' and the validator's >=2-source tolerance-check pattern, the safer design is: collector fetches the raw press-release HTML/text into reports/raw/ each quarter (mechanical, low-risk), and a human (or the validator, reading the rawExcerpt) transcribes the actual share % into data/*.json rather than trusting an automated regex parse as ground truth. Company IR/SEC filings do not supply the quantified % and are not a workable substitute.

nand-pricing.reasoning: No key-less, machine-readable (CSV/JSON) endpoint was found that returns actual DRAM/NAND contract or spot price LEVELS. The primary source (DRAMeXchange/TrendForce) gates the priced, per-part-number tables behind paid 'Gold+' membership; the free layer is limited to summary charts/indices of unconfirmed depth and to prose QoQ%-change commentary in press releases (same fragile-HTML pattern as memory-share). The one genuinely key-less numeric time series found (BLS/FRED semiconductor PPI) is too broad a category to stand in for DRAM/NAND pricing specifically. Recommend this domain stay a manual/curated quarterly entry sourced from the TrendForce press-center commentary (percentage change only, not absolute price) with the collector recording the rawExcerpt for validator self-verification, same as the memory-share domain — do not build an automated price-level scraper against this data source.
